brief.head: Marriage, unbundled
brief.text: Two cen­turies ago mar­riage bun­dled sex, com­pan­ion­ship, ro­mance, par­ent­hood and friend­ship, Amit Varma said; re­cent decades have brought what he calls the great un­bundling. {106-C11}

brief.head: Editing grown-ups
brief.text: A friendly virus fix­ing the mi­to­chon­dria in mus­cle cells could cure type 2 di­a­betes for life, Ajay Shah said. He ex­pects edits not just to em­bryos but to liv­ing adults. {106-C15}

brief.head: Refine it out there
brief.text: Don’t tow as­ter­oids home, Ajay Shah said; that is like haul­ing a coal mine’s waste. Build ro­botic fac­to­ries in the as­ter­oid belt and ship back re­fined metal. {106-C17}

brief.head: The idle car
brief.text: A self-driving car that moves all day matches a metro’s ef­fi­ciency, Ajay Shah said, and goes door to door. A pri­vately owned car mostly sits idle. {106-C21}

brief.head: The fertility puzzle
brief.text: Social ac­cep­tance of births out­side mar­riage, good child­care and re­pro­duc­tive tech­nol­ogy: coun­tries strong on all three, Ajay Shah said, will end up with more chil­dren. {106-C22}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah look 25 years ahead
lead.head: Forecast now, apologise in 2050

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 106

body: Just be­fore the cam­eras rolled, Ajay Shah con­fessed to the great tragedy of his life: he has lost his op­ti­mism for in­ter­stel­lar travel. Amit Varma, whose worry on most days is get­ting from Andheri to Bandra, steered them some­where nearer: the world of 2050.

The ques­tion had come a cou­ple of months ear­lier, from their col­league Vaishnav, on a drive home after din­ner: what will the world look like in 30 years? Shah came up with five things on the spot. Varma, who says he has an eagle eye for con­tent, said: episode.

They set­tled on 2050, 25 years out, a good round fig­ure. Varma set out the caveat first: “When you’re fore­cast­ing the fu­ture, you often tend to over­es­ti­mate the short term, un­der­es­ti­mate the long term.” {106-C01}
To show how hard it is, he went back 35 years, to 1990, when he was 16, and asked what had changed since.
## Looking back to look ahead
Varma counted three changes: friends found by choice rather than ge­og­ra­phy, a post-scarcity world of songs, books and films, and ev­ery­day magic such as GPS and free video calls.
Shah added that India has caught up with the West in per­sonal con­sump­tion. The gap now lies in pub­lic goods: cleaner air, bet­ter crim­i­nal jus­tice, a less dan­ger­ous in­come tax. {106-C05}
## Amit’s five
Varma’s pre­dic­tions leant on AI, and he warned against judg­ing it by today’s ChatGPT. Artificial gen­eral in­tel­li­gence, he thinks, is about five years away.
By 2050, he said, the al­go­rithm will not just find our en­ter­tain­ment but make it, to suit each person’s tastes and moods. Technology will also learn to pro­duce feel­ings on de­mand.
Machines will meet our in­stru­men­tal needs, leav­ing human bonds more hon­est and live art more val­ued. Relationships will be remapped, and some cities will wel­come any­one with a job.
## Ajay’s ten

Shah promised “some more pedes­trian things”, and de­liv­ered ten. Some were mod­est: he would like a brain-machine in­ter­face that runs re­gres­sions in his head and searches his own ar­chive of mil­lions of words.
Others were sweep­ing. Solar and wind, he said, will push the mar­ket price of elec­tric­ity to zero for hours of the day. {106-C14}

War will be fought by ma­chines, which could make wars eas­ier to end: “If they’re just ma­chines fly­ing and killing ma­chines, then you will ex­pend pres­sure, but you will not ex­pend blood.” {106-C18}
Meat will come from re-engineered bac­te­ria and algae, and a fer­tilised egg may be­come a new­born in­side a ma­chine.

Their sharpest dis­agree­ment came on cli­mate. Shah ex­pects rises of 2.5 to 3 de­grees to be baked in. Varma said he would “ve­he­mently and vi­o­lently dis­agree”, and in­voked “the great econ­o­mist Ajay Shah” in his sup­port.
Alarmism, Varma ar­gued, fol­lows fund­ing, and cheap en­ergy and nu­clear power will solve the prob­lem. {106-C25}
Shah’s rec­om­men­da­tion was a les­son in mod­esty: John Maynard Keynes’s 1930 essay *Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren*, much of which did not work out.
Varma saw brav­ery in it. Anyone pre­dict­ing the fu­ture, he said, knows they will get it re­ally wrong. “And yet he did it. And yet we did it.”
If the show is still around, their first episode of 2050 will be on what they got wrong.

second.label: Interstellar travel
second.head: Physics let him down
second.deck: Ajay Shah, born in 1966, mourns the breakthroughs his lifetime never brought

pic.caption: Apollo 11 crew Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Edwin Aldrin in 1969

body: Alpha Centauri is four and a half light years away, Ajay Shah said, and he sees no way to make the trip in under a thou­sand years. {#lightyears} That leaves a ro­botic probe, or hu­mans in a fully self-sustaining ecosys­tem.

As a young man he treated physics as mal­leable: surely worm­holes, surely ways past the speed of light. Born in 1966, he counts the hun­dred years be­fore his birth as sparkling, with physics chang­ing how we saw the world every decade. His own life, he said, has been “a waste­land of dull physics”. {106-S01}
Amit Varma was less cos­mic. Most days, he said, his worry on leav­ing home is how to get to Bandra from Andheri. {106-J02}

quote.text: So the great dis­ap­point­ment of my life is this feel­ing that the physics just never hap­pened.

third.head: Talk that came true

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Bill Gates’s bet on voice recognition

body: Long ago, Ajay Shah re­called, Bill Gates said in an in­ter­view that voice recog­ni­tion was com­ing. Shah was scep­ti­cal. “I said, like what? Voice recog­ni­tion? It’s so dif­fi­cult. But you know what? Actually the AI hap­pened.” {106-S07}
Gates could not have known which AI was in the pipe­line, Shah said. Now he ex­pects it to cope even with “a thick Bengali ac­cent”. Amit Varma: “Unnecessary.”

Hence Shah’s con­fi­dence in brain-machine in­ter­faces. He wants re­gres­sions in his head, and his ar­chive of mil­lions of words on tap: “I just want my own in­for­ma­tion de­liv­ered back to me be­cause then I ain’t for­get­ting.” {106-C16}

Varma has com­posed sym­phonies in his head since he was seven or eight, but never be­came a mu­si­cian: “I was too freak­ing lazy to learn an in­stru­ment.” {106-S08} An in­ter­face could fi­nally play his music as he imag­ines it.

p2.title: Fifteen bets on 2050
p2.deck: Amit Varma made five predictions and Ajay Shah ten, after a look back at 1990. {106-C01}

quote.text: many of the things we have nor­mal­ized and take for granted in our ev­ery­day lives are ac­tu­ally mag­i­cal.

box.title: A genius’s forecast, revisited
box.text: In 1930 John Maynard Keynes wrote *Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren*. Ajay Shah’s rec­om­men­da­tion: one of the smartest peo­ple in his­tory tried hard to fore­see pro­duc­tiv­ity, and much of it did not work out. A les­son for fu­tur­ists. {106-R12}

sections.label: Looking back
sections.head: Magic we stopped noticing
sections.caption: the world since 1990
body: To fore­cast 2050 with some hu­mil­ity, Amit Varma first went back 35 years, to 1990, when he was 16, and asked what had changed since. He found three things he could not have seen com­ing.

The first is com­mu­ni­ties of choice. Before the in­ter­net, friends came from ge­og­ra­phy: school, col­lege, the work­place. “The sur­face area of serendip­ity is low,” he said. {106-C02} Most of his dear friends are peo­ple he could not oth­er­wise have met. Even he and Ajay Shah, both in Bombay, would never have crossed paths.

The sec­ond is a post-scarcity world in bits and bytes. Making a mix­tape, or track­ing down a Van Morrison album after hear­ing one song, was once hard work. Now any song, book or film is a mo­ment away. {106-C03}
## Everyday magic

The third is Arthur C. Clarke’s third law: any suf­fi­ciently ad­vanced tech­nol­ogy is in­dis­tin­guish­able from magic. Never being lost, thanks to GPS, would have seemed utopian in 1990. As a stu­dent in the late 1980s, Varma queued at an STD booth out­side the Fergusson College hos­tel in Pune to call his par­ents. {106-S04} Now he can video-call loved ones any­where in the world.

~ Shah added the com­puter rev­o­lu­tion, which he thinks peo­ple still do not suf­fi­ciently ap­pre­ci­ate. The phone in our hand, he said, is more pow­er­ful than the world’s most pow­er­ful su­per­com­puter of twenty years ago. {#supercomputer}

quote.text: many of the things we have nor­mal­ized and take for granted in our ev­ery­day lives are ac­tu­ally mag­i­cal.

sections.label: Art and feeling
sections.head: Your mood, made to order
sections.caption: entertainment and feelings on demand
body: Amit Varma’s first pre­dic­tion: by 2050, most of our en­ter­tain­ment will be gen­er­ated by AI from our pref­er­ences. Technology first helped art scale, giv­ing us a Hollywood, a Bollywood and a Tollywood; now it splin­ters cul­ture into niches. “I pre­dict that the al­go­rithm will even be the cre­ator it­self,” he said. {106-C07}

Ajay Shah won­dered whether the bil­lions of items al­ready out there might cover every taste, leav­ing plat­forms only to find yours. Their game, he said, is all our spare at­ten­tion: as Netflix ex­ec­u­tives once put it, “we’re com­pet­ing with sleep”. {106-J19} Varma in­sisted that what he wants does not yet exist.
## Feelings on tap

His sec­ond pre­dic­tion fol­lowed from the first. Songs, med­i­ta­tion and drugs are all tech­nolo­gies for putting the brain in par­tic­u­lar states, and blunt ones. Once AI un­der­stands the brain, even as a black box, we could sum­mon peace, focus or hap­pi­ness di­rectly, and per­haps treat chronic de­pres­sion or ADHD. {106-C08}
Robert Nozick’s thought ex­per­i­ment, *The Experience Machine*, ar­gued that we would still choose the real world. Nozick is one of Varma’s favourite thinkers, but here he dis­agrees. {106-R01}

~ Shah fore­saw tremen­dous philo­soph­i­cal chal­lenges. If a but­ton could change how we feel, he said, we would have to de­cide what we would like to feel. He ad­mit­ted he would be be­wil­dered. {106-C09}

quote.text: the world is a tech­nol­ogy for mak­ing us feel a par­tic­u­lar way. A song is a ma­chine that makes me feel a par­tic­u­lar way.

sections.label: Machines and people
sections.head: Live, and in the flesh
sections.caption: deeper bonds with machines and people
body: Amit Varma’s third pre­dic­tion: deeper con­nec­tions with both ma­chines and peo­ple. He would wel­come an AI com­pan­ion like the spirit an­i­mals of Philip Pullman’s *Northern Lights* tril­ogy, and a vir­tual Ajay Shah to give ad­vice “so I can con­ve­niently ig­nore it”. {106-J05}

If sex dolls and ma­chines meet in­stru­men­tal needs, he ar­gued, con­ver­sa­tions be­tween peo­ple can turn to what re­ally mat­ters. He re­spects lust more than love, be­cause lust is hon­est; love may be a ra­tio­nal­i­sa­tion.
## Art in per­son

Art goes the same way. AI may take away the val­i­da­tion artists get, but not the joy of cre­at­ing or of live con­nec­tion. Ticket prices for stand-up shows and con­certs, he pre­dicted, will go up. {106-C10}

Shah was in Bombay when Beethoven’s Ninth was first per­formed in India. “My ears could tell there were flaws in the per­for­mance. But the point was that there were peo­ple who put it to­gether.” {106-S06}
~ His worry is the money. Live art might end up like a school show, with par­ents dragged in to ap­plaud: “re­ally the world’s worst hours that any par­ent has had to spend”. {106-J06}

quote.text: The idea of stand up com­edy is not that you tell me a joke which I laugh at. The laugh­ing is not the point.

sections.label: Global cities
sections.head: A job is the only visa
sections.caption: truly global cities
body: Amit Varma’s fifth pre­dic­tion is truly global cities. If you get a job some­where, he said, you should be able to go there: no in­ter­view, no visa. Migrants from Bihar and UP who drive Mumbai’s taxis make ev­ery­one bet­ter off.
Dubai, Singapore and the Hong Kong of old show the way, with low taxes and no na­tion­al­ism. “Openness can be their com­par­a­tive ad­van­tage,” he said. {106-C12}

Ajay Shah sketched a darker ver­sion: cos­mopoli­tan cities be­hind walls, bar­bar­ians at the gates, drones on guard. He also cited the pan­demic-era dig­i­tal nomad visas of Estonia and Portugal, which ask only for a sta­ble work-from-home in­come. But he doubts Dubai: re­mote work­ers choose for life, peo­ple, weather and cul­ture, “not a hot desert”.
## Money by the­o­rem

Varma ex­pects a global cur­rency, a suc­ces­sor to Bitcoin, which he called “a proto-something”. Shah agreed, for his own rea­sons. Central banks failed for cen­turies, he said; only in 1987 did New Zealand get to in­fla­tion tar­get­ing. {#nz}

~ In a Trump world, can the US Fed be trusted? World GDP, Shah said, is too big to rest on one country’s frag­ile in­sti­tu­tions. Crypto today has grifters and Trump coin, but he ex­pects 25 years of real in­no­va­tion. {106-C13}

quote.text: if you can re­move frail human in­sti­tu­tions and re­place them by cold the­o­rems and al­go­rithms, then you’ve added value to the world.

sections.label: Cheap power
sections.head: Sunshine on the house
sections.caption: free electricity
body: Nuclear power was once sold as en­ergy too cheap to meter. Ajay Shah, as an econ­o­mist, said hold your horses: the plants are ex­tremely ex­pen­sive hard­ware, with high cap­i­tal costs.

The dom­i­nant force, he said, is solar and wind, rid­ing ex­pe­ri­ence curves through small gains. He had just read that an un­der­grad­u­ate had solved the equa­tions of wind­mill blades bet­ter, for gains of 1 or 2 per cent. {#windmill}
India’s best wind sites, he noted, are off­shore be­yond Tamil Nadu and in a ring around Sri Lanka. {#offshore}
## Free for hours

With cheap bat­ter­ies and time-of-day pric­ing, power will be dear in the evening but free in the sunny hours. What would we do, he asked, if elec­tric­ity were free for sig­nif­i­cant chunks of the day? {106-C14}
His triv­ial ex­am­ple: de­sali­nate sea­wa­ter all along the coast in those hours. And no­body in their good mind in India, he said, should be putting up fos­sil-fuel ca­pac­ity.
~ Amit Varma pointed lis­ten­ers to their episode on the fu­ture of elec­tric­ity, one of the show’s best in his view, and to the one on nu­clear power.

quote.text: I’m say­ing we have not con­fronted the stag­ger­ing con­se­quences of the word zero.

sections.label: The disagreement
sections.head: Two degrees of separation
sections.caption: climate change
body: Ajay Shah is op­ti­mistic about re­new­ables but gloomy about the air. Carbon diox­ide, he said, takes about a thou­sand years to go away, so the stock mat­ters, not just today’s emis­sions. {#co2}

We are at about 1.5 de­grees of warm­ing over pre-industrial times, roughly as the mod­els pre­dicted, and the oceans delay the full ef­fect by 20 to 40 years. “So I think two point five or three de­gree rises in the tem­per­a­ture are kinda baked in.” {106-C24}

The world once fixed the ozone layer by phas­ing out CFCs, he re­called, and India did not de­mand 20 more years of Freon. Without American lead­er­ship, he sees no such deal on car­bon, which needs a com­men­su­rate tax. {106-S11}
## The dis­sent

Amit Varma agreed that warm­ing is real and caused by hu­mans, but said it is less se­vere than claimed and will be solved. Climate NGOs, he ar­gued, are funded for pre­dict­ing dystopia, so they ex­ag­ger­ate. {106-C25}
He cited Al Gore’s failed ten-year fore­casts, Bjorn Lomborg’s books and France, which is 71 per cent nu­clear and emits a tenth of the world av­er­age car­bon diox­ide per kilo­watt hour. {#france}
~ Shah’s own pic­ture of 2050 is of peo­ple shel­ter­ing in­side steel struc­tures, keep­ing the weather out.

quote.text: That kind of global co­or­di­na­tion is no longer avail­able. We no longer have American lead­er­ship.
When we read these books, we are not just spec­u­lat­ing on some­thing that is in the fu­ture and may or may not hap­pen. We are spec­u­lat­ing on the present be­cause the fu­ture is here.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: From a Russian airfield to Tolstoy’s dining room, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Ukraine’s raid on Russia’s strategic bombers
stories.head: The day the truck roofs opened
body: Ajay Shah called it “one of the most au­da­cious and in­no­va­tive and bril­liant at­tacks in the his­tory of war­fare”, and walked through how Ukraine pulled it off. {106-S10}
First, 117 drones with ex­plo­sive pay­loads of per­haps 3 to 5 kg were smug­gled into Russia, prob­a­bly across the Chinese or Kazakh bor­der, where check­ing is low.
In a safe house, re­port­edly right next to an FSB build­ing, they were as­sem­bled and loaded into con­tain­ers on trucks. The tops of the con­tain­ers could re­tract.

Unwitting Russian driv­ers were told to take the trucks to set GPS co­or­di­nates and step out. They du­ti­fully fol­lowed Google Maps to four or five bases. Five to ten kilo­me­tres from the air­fields, the roofs opened.

The drones flew at about 50 km an hour, the peak speed of birds, so de­fend­ers took time to tell what they were. {#fiftykph} They used the or­di­nary 4G net­work over a VPN home, and the crews were al­ready safely in­side Ukraine.

Ukraine claims 41 strate­gic bombers and AWACS planes de­stroyed, worth about $7 bil­lion; in­de­pen­dent es­ti­mates con­firm 21. If the 41 is right, about 34 per cent of Russia’s strate­gic bomber fleet is gone. Many of these air­craft are no longer made, and Russia lacks the fac­to­ries to make them.
The bill, by Shah’s rough reck­on­ing: two lakh dol­lars of drones, about $2 mil­lion all in. {#twomillion}
~ Then the fear. “It’s like 9-11,” Shah said. Once it has been done, the genie is out of the bot­tle.
stories.why: A few mil­lion dol­lars de­stroyed bil­lions in as­sets that can­not be re­placed. Amit Varma’s worry is darker: cheap drone swarms could hit a crowd in Mumbai, and the fu­ture of war may be­come the fu­ture of ter­ror. {106-C19}
stories.postscript: Varma noted that such an at­tack was unimag­in­able and unim­ple­mentable as lit­tle as three years ago, born of ne­ces­sity in an ex­is­ten­tial war. {#threeyears}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Ukraine’s drone raid on Russia’s bombers

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a vegetarian host and meat without killing
stories.head: Aunt orders chicken, gets one
body: Leo Tolstoy was by then a veg­e­tar­ian, Amit Varma said, when his aunt an­nounced that she would come to din­ner and eat chicken and noth­ing else. {106-S09}
She came. In the din­ing room she found a live chicken on her chair. You want a chicken, Tolstoy told her: here it is. Kill it, cook it, then eat it.

Varma once wrote an essay called *Tolstoy’s Chicken*, so long ago that it no longer ex­ists. He loves meat and thinks it nec­es­sary for health, but dis­likes the thought of being re­spon­si­ble for killing an­i­mals.
~ Lab-grown meat would end that dilemma for him. Ajay Shah’s rea­son to ex­pect it by 2050: “it’s cheaper to get an E. coli to make a mus­cle cell than to grow a cow or a goat.” {106-C20}

quote.text: the dif­fer­ence be­tween the chicken on the chair and the chicken on the plate.

stories.postscript: Varma also cited Matt Ridley’s spec­u­la­tion that Homo sapi­ens ate Neanderthals, and won­dered whether human meat could be grown in a lab. {106-J23}

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on landing in America in the late 1980s
stories.head: All the theory, none of the CDs
body: In the late 1980s Ajay Shah caught a plane to Los Angeles to do a PhD; by then, fly­ing was stan­dard. Montek Ahluwalia, he re­called, had been among the last co­horts to go to study in Britain by boat from Bombay, up the Red Sea. {106-S02}
“In the late 80s, India was truly back­ward,” Shah said. His mid­dle-class par­ents were early adopters of every new thing, yet America was full of firsts.
He saw his first CD player and his first CD. “I read in­nu­mer­able is­sues of IEEE Spectrum, and I was a com­plete en­thu­si­ast about CDs, but I’d never touched a CD be­fore.” {106-S03}
~ He saw dahi sold in boxes, when Indians al­ways made their own at home, and high­ways at 100 kph. Stepping into LAX felt like en­ter­ing a sci­ence fic­tion city.
stories.why: Then, going abroad made India feel back­ward. Today, Shah said, the Indian elite con­sume at the global state of the art; the West’s lead is in pub­lic goods, such as cleaner air and bet­ter crim­i­nal jus­tice. {106-C05}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s reply: “We had CD bars in India on the high­ways.”

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his first CD, in America

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what the machines really did to chess
stories.head: Engines broke the Soviet mould
body: When en­gines grew stronger than the world’s best player, Amit Varma said, ev­ery­one as­sumed chess was solved and would die, or turn into mem­o­ris­ing com­puter lines, with ev­ery­one play­ing alike. Exactly the op­po­site hap­pened.

Before, nearly ev­ery­body played in one style, built on the Soviet school’s shared heuris­tics. “AI al­lowed you to find con­crete ex­cep­tions to ab­stract prin­ci­ples that were in gen­eral good,” Varma said. {106-S05}
Many play­ers also learned straight from the ma­chines, not from the same books and cir­cuits. Hence Wesley So, Nakamura and Giri, whose styles dif­fer sharply from one an­other.
~ Games now pair deeper prepa­ra­tion with more orig­i­nal play over the board, as play­ers lure op­po­nents into sec­ond- and third-best lines they have not pre­pared.
stories.why: Machines can deepen human en­gage­ment in­stead of re­plac­ing it. That is Varma’s model for 2050: let ma­chines meet in­stru­men­tal needs, and human re­la­tion­ships and live art grow more hon­est and more val­ued. {106-C10}

quiz.q: Which law, cited by Amit Varma, says advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic?
quiz.a: Arthur C. Clarke’s third law, which he ap­plied to GPS and video calls.

quiz.q: How big a market for computers did IBM’s Thomas Watson foresee, as Varma quoted him?
quiz.a: A world mar­ket for three com­put­ers at most: a warn­ing about judg­ing early AI.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah think robotic warfare could make wars easier to stop?
quiz.a: Only ma­chines are de­stroyed, so no blood is spilt and bat­tle­field facts be­come clear.

quiz.q: What simple use did Shah suggest for hours when India’s electricity costs nothing?
quiz.a: Desalinating sea­wa­ter all along the coast to pro­duce very large sup­plies of water.

quiz.q: Which global problem did the world once solve together, and why does Shah doubt a repeat?
quiz.a: The ozone layer, by phas­ing out CFCs; American lead­er­ship is no longer avail­able.

quiz.q: What Unix command did Ajay Shah want to run on his own brain?
quiz.a: Grep, a tool for search­ing text files, like a menu for steaks.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 106. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Leo Tolstoy (Sergei Prokudin-Gorskii, public domain); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Apollo 11 (NASA, public domain); Arthur C. Clarke (ITU Pictures, CC BY 2.0); Robert Nozick (Libertarian Review, public domain); Margaret Atwood (Collision Conf, CC BY 2.0).

shelf.title: The Experience Machine
shelf.creator: Robert Nozick
shelf.why: Nozick is one of Amit’s favourite thinkers, but here Amit dis­agrees with him.

shelf.title: His Dark Materials (the Northern Lights trilogy)
shelf.creator: Philip Pullman
shelf.why: Books Amit calls mas­ter­pieces, ask­ing you to trust him blindly; years later they still make him smile or tear up.

shelf.title: The Moral Animal
shelf.creator: Robert Wright
shelf.why: Amit’s pick among books on nat­u­ral se­lec­tion be­cause it deals with moral­ity: how evo­lu­tion pro­duced our bet­ter in­stincts (it taught him ‘re­cip­ro­cal altruism’) and how mar­riage evolved, with monogamy and polygamy as adap­ta­tions to dif­fer­ent cir­cum­stances.

shelf.title: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
shelf.why: Amit’s most pop­u­lar Seen and the Unseen episode, a con­ver­sa­tion with Shrayana Bhattacharya (who gave him the ‘anti-uncle’ label) on the eco­nomic and so­cial lives of Indian women.

shelf.title: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates (2008)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s provoca­tive ar­gu­ment that ris­ing di­vorce rates, often lamented as ‘be­com­ing like the West’, show more women gain­ing the agency and means to leave bad mar­riages.

shelf.title: Malini Goyal is the Curious One (Episode 377, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Malini Goyal
shelf.why: Journalist Malini Goyal on Bangalore: her di­ag­no­sis of a city with 5G soft­ware and 2G hard­ware, and her re­search on its dat­ing cul­ture, which found that when ev­ery­one has ten choices, peo­ple who want a part­ner to grow with strug­gle to find one.

shelf.title: Genetic Engineering (Episode 165, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shambhavi Naik
shelf.why: Amit calls it an ex­cel­lent episode with Shambhavi Naik of Takshashila.

shelf.title: What Just Happened Between India & Pakistan? (Episode 418, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Aditya Ramanathan
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion recorded as events un­folded, with Pranay Kotasthane and Aditya Ramanathan, on the lat­est India-Pakistan clash, which showed both sides using fairly ad­vanced equip­ment.

shelf.title: Sell the Tiger to Save It (2006)
shelf.creator: Barun Mitra
shelf.why: Barun Mitra’s ar­gu­ment, against the re­flex to ban ev­ery­thing, that le­gal­is­ing the tiger trade would give peo­ple a rea­son to breed tigers as they breed cows and chick­ens, and so save the species.

shelf.title: It is immoral to have children. Here’s why (2017)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s de­lib­er­ately provoca­tive col­umn: we agree not to act on peo­ple with­out con­sent, cause pain or kill, yet a child is born with­out con­sent and will suf­fer and die.

shelf.title: False Alarm (and Bjorn Lomborg’s books generally)
shelf.creator: Bjorn Lomborg
shelf.why: Amit says the alarmist pre­dic­tions of past decades, in­clud­ing Al Gore’s ten-year fore­casts, turned out wrong.

shelf.title: Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren (1930)
shelf.creator: John Maynard Keynes
shelf.why: One of the smartest peo­ple in his­tory tried hard to pre­dict fu­ture pro­duc­tiv­ity, and much of it didn’t work out.

shelf.title: Ex Machina
shelf.creator: Alex Garland
shelf.why: A film that asks whether some­thing we cre­ate that ap­proaches con­scious­ness has rights: if an AGI is con­scious by every def­i­ni­tion we use, why should being made of bits rather than or­ganic mat­ter deny it moral stand­ing?

shelf.title: The Tesseract
shelf.creator: Alex Garland
shelf.why: The Beach is Garland’s more fa­mous novel, but Amit prefers The Tesseract and calls it fan­tas­tic.

shelf.title: Blade Runner 2049
shelf.creator: Denis Vileneuve
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite films, which he loves even more than Ridley Scott’s orig­i­nal mas­ter­piece: a mag­nif­i­cent med­i­ta­tion on the shap­ing of the self and the na­ture of mem­ory.

shelf.title: The science fiction of Margaret Atwood, Ursula Le Guin, Ted Chiang and Ken Liu
shelf.creator: Margaret Atwood, Ursula Le Guin, Ted Chiang, Ken Liu
shelf.why: People dis­miss sci­ence fic­tion as genre en­ter­tain­ment.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on The Future of Electricity
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on the power sec­tor: solar, wind, stor­age and time-of-day pric­ing, why elec­tric­ity prices must be al­lowed to move, and why fix­ing Indian power is a 25-year jour­ney that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing de­pends on.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on nuclear power
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case for nu­clear power as a path out of fos­sil fuels: Amit calls it the safest form of en­ergy known and an ob­vi­ous an­swer to cli­mate change, point­ing to France, which at 71% nu­clear emits a tenth of the world av­er­age CO2 per kilo­watt hour.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on cycling
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s pas­sion for pro­fes­sional cy­cling, which he says will re­main ‘the great­est sport on earth’ even when au­ton­o­mous cars take over, be­cause human en­deav­our, char­ac­ter and dif­fi­culty don’t go away.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything Episode 2 (on AI)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ early episode on AI, with Amit’s ar­gu­ment that AGI is about five years away and eas­ier to reach than peo­ple as­sume.

laughs.text: Amit de­flates the in­ter­stel­lar gloom: ‘Bro, you are a big, big thinker. Most days my worry if I leave my home is how do I get to Bandra from Andheri.’
Ajay boasts that his pants, shirt and watch match any­thing in the West. Amit: ‘Not just your pants, not just your shirt, not just your watch, your per­son­al­ity is world class.’

On al­go­rithms find­ing your kink: ‘what­ever my kinks are, and I will not tell you about my kinks’. Moments later, after imag­in­ing a film with only de­cap­i­ta­tion: ‘I don’t know why I got to de­cap­i­ta­tion, it’s not my kink.’
Amit wants an AI ver­sion of Ajay for when the real one is busy, one that can tell him what ad­vice Ajay would give ‘so I can con­ve­niently ig­nore it.’
After prais­ing Dubai’s am­bi­tions to be a global hub: ‘If you run Dubai, get in touch with me, I have ideas.’

Amit on gene edit­ing: ‘I edited my genes in 1992.’ He was eigh­teen, ‘fully grunge and Nirvana Pearl Jam’, and wanted torn jeans, so he ripped them him­self. ‘I ripped the code. So I’ve been there done that.’

After Ajay dreams of run­ning grep on his own brain, Amit says: ‘the first thing I’m going to Google from my head? I’m going to Google the word grep.’ Ajay ex­plains it as a Unix com­mand for search­ing text files, e.g. ‘let me grep in this restau­rant menu for all the steaks.’
On hu­mans writ­ing code far from the front while ro­bots fight: ‘So the macho IIT-ian gets his fan­tasies ful­filled with­out putting him­self in dan­ger.’ Ajay: ‘Correct.’
Ajay pic­tures a quad­copter taxi wait­ing at Amit’s 21st-floor win­dow. Amit: ‘And I will miss and I will fall down.’
Arthur C. Clarke’s third law, ‘any suf­fi­ciently ad­vanced tech­nol­ogy is in­dis­tin­guish­able from magic’, ap­plied to GPS, video calls and Neuralink.
IBM chief Thomas Watson’s fa­mous line, quoted by Amit as ‘I think there’s a world mar­ket for three com­put­ers at most’, as a warn­ing against judg­ing a tech­nol­ogy by its early form.
Netflix executives’ re­mark that ‘we’re com­pet­ing with sleep’, cited by Ajay to de­scribe tech com­pa­nies chas­ing 100% of our at­ten­tion.
Al Gore’s doc­u­men­tary, cited by Amit as a fore­cast whose ten-year pre­dic­tions ‘turned out to be com­pletely wrong’.
